utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: A very good morning to everybody. Please be seated. Can we hear the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning. This is Case Number IT-97-24-T, the Prosecutor versus Milomir Stakic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And the appearances.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Nicholas Koumjian with Ruth Karper for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, Branko Lukic, John Ostojic, and Danilo Cirkovic for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask, I received the amended proffer related to Defence Witness 053. So therefore, I take it we will start with this witness. And any protective measures?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We start with this witness, and no protective measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I can see no other matters to be discussed immediately. So may I ask the usher to escort the witness into the courtroom. In the meantime, could the Defence please indicate the following order after having heard number 053. What will be the calling order for the week?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The next one is 079, and we don't have numbers for the rest. So we'll give it to you on the break because they are not here yet. We have only two witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes. If you could inform us immediately after the first break.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Marjanovic. Can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Could you then please be so kind and give us your solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Please take your seat. You are a witness called by the Defence. Mr. Lukic, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Marjanovic.

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: For the record, my name is Branko Lukic. Together with Mr. John Ostojic and Danilo Cirkovic, I represent Dr. Stakic before the Tribunal in The Hague. Would you please be so kind and also for the record state your name.

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Ostoja Marjanovic. My father's name is Nikola. I was born on the 17th of February, 1942, in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Where do you currently reside?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: I currently reside in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Where did you reside between 1991 and 1996?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: I lived in the town in Dzemala Bijedica Street. Currently the name of this street is Majora Tepica Street.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What is your profession, Mr. Marjanovic?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: I graduated in mining, so I am a mining engineer. I was over 30 years of experience in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When did you graduate from the university, and where was that?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: I graduated in 1969 in Belgrade. And I returned to the Ljubija mine in Prijedor where I spent all my working life until this very day.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you please give us some information about your career in the iron mine -- iron ore mine in Ljubija from the day you started working until the moment you stopped working in the mine.

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to tell you briefly everything I did from 1997 -- 1970. I started as a shift leader. Then I started working on the Omarska project between 1974 and 1979. In 1979 I became the technical director of the central mine, that is one segment of the Ljubija mine. That's where I spent five years. Between 1985 and 1989, I worked as the director of the development sector in the Ljubija mine. And then in 1990, I applied for the position of the CEO of the Ljubija mine, and I was appointed on the 1st of February, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were you ever a member of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was a member of the SDS from the -- October of 1983 until 1st August, 1994. And I also at the time held the position of the vice-president of the Executive Board of the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor. That was a volunteer position. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were you a member of a committee or a board or a commission at the time?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was. I was appointed to the committee on information or propaganda. I don't know what the name of that committee was. I remember we had one unsuccessful meeting because I did not agree with the concept put forth by the president of that committee. I believe that his name was Kantar. And after that, I was never invited to any of the meetings of that committee.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please, Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Perhaps -- Mr. Cirkovic is pointing it out that the witness -- the translation was the witness was a member of SDS October 1983. I don't know if counsel wants to clarify that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think the entire question should be repeated, also the next sentence is difficult to understand, or the next two sentences.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Marjanovic, sometimes it happens that things are not recorded in the transcript or are omitted from the transcript. So I would kindly ask you to slow down a little, relax. Can you please repeat the dates, that is the time period during which you were a member of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I will tell you about my political engagement. Even before that time, and I believe that you will then be able to understand the confusion that has arisen. I was a member of the League of Communists until 1988. Then I left the ranks of that party of my own will. I was not a member of any party because at that time, the parties that were formed upheld the concept that I was not in favour of. I was a member of the SDS from October 1993 until the 1st of August, 1994. During that period of time, I was a member of the committee on information or propaganda. I really don't remember its exact title. Only one meeting of that committee was held, that is to say, I attended only one meeting of that committee. I did not agree with the concept of the work of that committee. And after that, I was never invited to any of the meetings of that committee.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It is also unclear, what was your position? Sorry. It was also unclear, what was your position as a volunteer?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: I was in the position of the vice-president of the Executive Board of the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor. And that was from October 1993 until the 1st of August, 1994. I was a vice-president of the Executive Board, and this was a voluntary position.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: During that period of time, were you also a member of the armed forces of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: On the 1st of November, 1992, I volunteered and joined the air force of Republika Srpska. And I worked in the air force until 1996. I think that it is exceptionally important for me to explain to you that during this period of time, I was also in the position of the CEO of the iron ore mine, and that was throughout all this period, save for the time that I spent in the Executive Board.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were you in the army? And when you were in the army, were you also in the position of the CEO of the Ljubija mine?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is exactly what I've just said. I've told you that besides being a member of the air force, I continued holding the position of the CEO of the Ljubija mine, and that I did that throughout the entire period save for the period of time that I spent in the position of the vice-president of the Executive Board.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The air force of Republika Srpska, and when you were there, what was your duty? What tasks did you have and what duties did you discharge in the air force of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm a sports pilot, and the aircraft that I flew on was the aircraft of the sports club that existed in Prijedor. They are two-seater airplanes with the strength of the engine of 220 horsepower. When I joined the air force, I was charged with looking after these aircraft in Prijedor and to be engaged in the civilian part of the organisation of the newly established air force base in Mahovljani. That is some 20 kilometres away from Banja Luka. And the civilians' duties consisted of the following: I organised the maintenance of the vehicles there -- not the aircraft but the vehicles. Also to organise the food for the people, to organise the monitored [indiscernable], bearing in mind the huge rate of inflation that prevailed at that time. I believe I have given you a good enough explanation of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, you did indeed. Thank you. Can you also tell us, please, what was your ethnic background? How did you declare yourself during the last census in 1991 and before that?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: If I remember it well, there was a census in 1971, and then another one in 1991. I declared myself as a Yugoslav.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: After the personal data, we are now going to move on to the area for which you have been called as a witness. We would kindly ask you to tell us what you know about the period before the conflict, during the conflict, and after the conflict. I would now kindly ask you to focus on the period before April 1992. Are you aware of the fact that the transmitter on Kozara was taken over and who was it who took it over? This was the transmitter that transmitted a TV signal for the area of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: The transmitter on Kozara, in addition to the tower that transmitted TV signals also contained some military equipment, some air force military equipment. As far as I know, from what I heard in conversations with citizens of Prijedor, the tower was taken over by the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: After the takeover of this tower, could you watch TV Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: No, we couldn't watch any of the programmes from TV Sarajevo. We received information -- most of our information we received from radio and television Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So it was possible to follow the programmes of Zagreb TV?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. We could do it. All the citizens who wanted to be informed could direct their antennas towards Sljeme mountain, and they could easily follow all the channels of Zagreb TV.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In late 1991, did you set up some sort of a movement? Were you at the head of some sort of a movement?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Bearing in mind everything that was going on in the territory of the former Yugoslavia, I thought that it was my duty and my obligation to try and work on the reconciliation of people, of neighbours of different ethnic backgrounds. Already at the time, one could feel exceptionally strong tensions. And already at the time, there was a division among people on ethnic grounds. I invited respectable representatives of various ethnic backgrounds, doctors, artists, workers. I invited them all to the management building of Ljubija, and I proposed to them that we should form a peace movement. This received a lot of support, and we appointed Dr. Eso Sadikovic as the leader of that movement. We held a few meetings in Prijedor. And at those meetings, people tried to alleviate those tensions, to reduce them. And to prevent the things that one could feel would happen eventually. Within that context, I asked party leaders, the leaders of the SDA, the HDZ, and the SDS, to come to Ljubija together with their closest associates, and the intention was for all of us to talk. I was going to ask them to go to the villages with mixed population and to the villages with a majority population of any ethnic background and to show them that there was unity, all that with a view to protecting the people and resources of Prijedor. There were also journalists amongst us. At that moment, I would say there were entrenched positions already felt. They had their hard-core positions that they defended as hard as they could. The president of the HDZ was my colleague from grammar school. I realised that they didn't want to give in. The meeting ended without any visible results. I remember one detail from that meeting which can illustrate the desire for reconciliation. I said that if anything should happen to me, if an accident should occur to me, I told them that it would be my neighbour who would help me sooner than Milosevic in Belgrade. This was published by journalist Nezirevic. I don't know where he is now. At the end of that meeting, I asked my colleague from grammar school to step into my office. We were alone, the two of us. His name was Silvester Saric. I told him -- I asked him, rather, "Why do you strictly adhere to your principles?" And he told me that he went to meetings in Zagreb, and that he simply has to do that. I didn't realise why, why he should maintain this position. I always considered him to be more responsible to the people in Prijedor than to people in Zagreb. Later on, this peace movement assumed a different form and was taken over by Jutel. Jutel was a newly established radio and television station headed by Goran Milic. I believe that it was Goran Milic who was the head of that station. They held a big meeting in Tuzla as far as I can remember. Later on, they organised the peace march, and they headed for Osijek. However, the result of that were a number of incidents and provocations and so on and so forth. What I'm talking about now I saw on television. I did not participate in that movement. Later on, that movement just ceased to exist spontaneously.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you propose that representatives of the parties address the public through radio or television, and what was their response to this?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I have already mentioned that this meeting was also attended by journalists. They wanted to interview the leading people in these parties, but they did not want to give them interviews. They did appear, or rather speak on Radio Prijedor, however, and there, they mostly advocated their party platforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was there a point in time when you organised people to go to the front in Croatia so that they would see what war was like and become aware of its dangers?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Excuse me. At that time, war was already raging in Slavonia and Croatia. There was some units from Prijedor in that war theatre, and I organised a bus from the mine to take these leading party figures to the area where war operations were going on. The places across the bridge, when you cross the bridge in Gradiska, there is a river called Strug where a bridge had been destroyed. And next to that bridge, there is a large village or something like that - I no longer recall its name - where the consequences of war operations were evident, and they were terrible. The houses had been burnt down. Everything was destroyed. There were bullet cases lying all around, tools scattered around, agricultural tools, and so on. There weren't many of us. There were around 15 of us. The leading people from the parties did not come. But there were representatives of the Muslim people, the Croatian people, and the Serbian people. I have a piece of information which might be interesting to show that my intention in going there failed. Dedo Crnalic, a great friend of mine, an acquaintance, an eminent sports worker in Prijedor, in a cafe where there were people who later told me this, he said in the presence of these people, he said: "Marjanovic thought he would frighten me if he showed me what was going on in Slavonia." I had expected anything but this from this friend of mine. And to this day, I don't know what led him to form this opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Before the 30th of April, 1992, were there any incidents in the municipality of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: No, there weren't any incidents, but it was quite clear to anyone walking about the town going to public places - and by this I mean restaurants, cafes, canteens - there was already a lot of tension among the people. And it was evident that there was division along ethnic lines. There was something malevolent in the area, but I don't recall any incidents. I don't think there were any.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you perhaps hear about the stopping of military convoys, provocations of the army, the then JNA?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We had occasion to watch this on television, and this happened almost everywhere in Croatia, and before that in Slovenia. And then in Bosnia-Herzegovina while the JNA was withdrawing, roads were blocked and there were provocations. This also happened in Prijedor. I think that a tank unit from Pancevo arrived in Prijedor, and there were already individual excesses. I know of some cases where Muslims were displeased by these incidents, rather --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter corrects herself. The Muslims said bad things about these units and called them various names.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were you a member of the Chamber of Commerce of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: For about two months, after I was appointed -- or rather, two months after I was appointed general director of the Ljubija mine, I was advised by the Chamber of Economy of Bosnia-Herzegovina that I had become a member. I attended a few meetings in Sarajevo. And I attended two or three meetings in Zenica where there was discussion of repairing RMK Zenica, which is a large metallurgy complex in Zenica, in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and Ljubija was part of this large complex. I was able to have discussions on the economy with Mr. Abdic who was delegated by the presidency to take charge of the economy. These were times of great difficulty in economic terms because inflation was very high, and there was no money available. We had a plant exporting clay to Italy. That was an exporter from Rijeka. And at that time, we lost some of our revenue because payments were not flowing smoothly, and this money was simply lost. There was some talk of a loan from Libya amounting to $60 million in order to rescue RMK Zenica. The mine had loans from the Soviet Union amounting to $50 million. We expected funds, and I have information that the first payment of $30 million arrived in Bosnia-Herzegovina; however, not a single dollar reached Prijedor. And subsequent events caused the complete stoppage of the work of this complex.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Marjanovic, for the sake of clarity, you say that your exporter was in Rijeka?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What republic is Rijeka in?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Rijeka is in Croatia. It's right below Istria, and it was convenient for us to work with them because we were exporting to Italy, and they were middlemen and in the immediate vicinity of Triest and Geneva where the offices of our buyers were.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The impossibility of collecting these payments, did this occur when war broke out in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Evidently, yes. I will try to clarify this further by saying that I instructed the commercial director and the technical director of the mine to go to Triest, but they had to travel by way of Hungary and Slovenia. That is how they reached Triest. And the buyer sent them a certain sum of money so that we could pay the wages of the workers employed in producing the clay that we exported to Italy.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At that time, you were at the head of the iron ore mine of Ljubija. Can you explain to us what sort of organisation this was, what its organisational units were, how later on the structure of this company changed.

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Iron ore mines, or rather, the Ljubija iron ore mines, on the 1st of February, 1991, had 4.630 employees. That was on the date when I was appointed general director of the Ljubija mine. I think I should say that the ethnic makeup of the employees in the mine was approximately as follows: About 1.100 Muslims; about 1.100 or 1.200 Croats; and the rest were Serbs. And of course, I was a Yugoslav. The organisation was rather complicated, but I will try to explain it to you. This was a complex organisation of associated labour where there were nine or ten basic associations -- basic organisations of associated labour which operated with their own management and which had all the characteristics of companies. That is, they had their managing director, the company secretary, foremen in the mines, leaders of the economic units, and so on and so forth. I was the president of the management board which consisted of the managing directors of the basic organisations of associated labour. I will try to give you more details. I apologise if I don't remember everything. The basic organisation of the central mines was in Ljubija. The basic organisation of associated labour of the eastern mines was in Busnovi or Tomasica. The basic organisation of associated labour of Omarska was in the Omarska, Lamovita, and Mariska local communes. The basic organisation of associated labour of administration, personnel, and general services. Then there was the maintenance and repair organisation. Then there was the basic organisation of associated labour of providing meals for the canteen. Then there was another basic organisation of mining works and working unit for bookkeeping and other administrative matters. Management system was one of subordination to the general director, that is, the president of the management board via the directors of the basic organisations of associated labour, and then the work units. The work units and the board of management were located in Prijedor in the street that used to be called Mosa Pijada Number 1. That was the headquarters. And the headquarters of the other basic organisation of associated labour were located in the plants. Do you feel that this is sufficient, or should I go into further detail?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will just try to remind you, was the company, or rather the basic organisation of associated labour as it was then Geoistrage, was it part of this organisation?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I apologise. I forgot to mention not only Geoistrage but also Unametal and Ferox. And I do apologise but it's hard for me to enumerate everything all at once. It may be interesting for me to say where these basic organisations were geographically in relation to the headquarters in Prijedor. Ljubija is about 12 kilometres away. Tomasica, or rather, the eastern mines is about 18 kilometres. Omarska was some 20 kilometres away. Unametal was some 5 kilometres away. Maintenance and repair were in the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think that all that remains for us to mention is the car servicing organisation of associated labour.

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But let me also mention that this system existed until the beginning of 1992 when by a decision of the board of management, some of these organisations, Unametal, Ferox, the canteens, and the mining and construction works were separated by a referendum of the employees. But the car servicing unit, the referendum was not -- did not come out in favour of separation. So the central mines, eastern mines, Omarska, and maintenance and repair and the car servicing unit remained.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Would the usher be so kind and show the witness Exhibit Number S15-16, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Marjanovic, do you recognise what is on this photograph?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I do recognise it, yes. This is the administration building of the Omarska mine with the canteen and the service workshop. That's this bigger building.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. What is the building on the left-hand side of the photograph?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Are you referring to this one?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: That -- rather, this is the administration building. This one here. And the smaller part is the canteen. And this big building, that is the service workshop. The road arriving from the north in this direction here, that's north, this road leads to the surface excavation site. And here you can see where the sludge accumulated, and this leads to the Medjudja site and the Medjudja sludge disposal area.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let's just clarify something. The road arriving in this complex, does it come from the east? If we look to the left, is that east or north?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: In my view, it's northeast/east, so it's more east than north. But it's not purely east, strictly east.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On the right-hand side of this big building, are there electric units?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: As I remember, because from 1974 to 1979, I was the leader of the project. There are some underground cables, some above-ground cables, and some posts. And as for these smaller buildings, I don't know what their purpose was. They were part of the complex. For the sake of clarification, Omarska was completed in 1984, and I stopped work on the project in 1979.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Although you can't see it on this photo, can you tell us whether in the area of these facilities that is covered by asphalt, are there lighting posts?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there are. I'm sure of that. To confirm what I'm saying, I would like to say that flying in a small Piper, I wanted to land there, but I couldn't because of the lighting posts.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Okay, thank you. We won't need the photograph any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You said that you were a member of the Chamber of Commerce of Bosnia-Herzegovina during the period before the outbreak of the conflict. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: I've said I was a member of the Chamber of Commerce of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And in 1991, I attended a few meetings. I also attended a few meetings with Mr. Abdic in Zenica. And at the end of 1991 and in the beginning of 1992, I did not receive any invitations for any of the meetings. I don't know whether they considered me to be a member of the Chamber of Commerce at the time or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Some things we absolutely understand because we come from the area. However, there are other participants in this trial, and that's why I may be asking you questions for which you will think that you have already answered them or that you imply things in your previous answers.

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: I will say that once again. In 1991, I attended a few meetings, but after that, I no longer received any invitations and I didn't attend any of the meetings of the Chamber of Commerce of Bosnia and Herzegovina after that, after the end of 1991, beginning 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You said that Mr. Abdic also participated in these meetings.

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What party did Mr. Abdic represent?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Abdic came to these meetings in Zenica on behalf of the presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and he was a member as far as I know of the SDA. He received a number, a large number of votes in the elections, and bearing in mind the number of votes that he received, he should have been the president of the presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I must explain, I'm not dissatisfied with your answer. I'm just waiting for the translation to be over. So, Mr. Abdic was also a member of the presidency of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He was a member of the presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina in charge of economic trends during that period of time in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Since he joined the presidency from a well-known company and a businessman with a reputation, his company name was Agrokomerc and that company was well-known in the former Yugoslavia and all over Europe. I would like to apologise to everybody for sometimes rush, and I especially apologise to the interpreters and to the court reporters for giving them a hard time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You've mention that had in the elections in 1990, Mr. Abdic got a huge number of votes and that he should have, therefore, become the president of the republic.

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know, what actually happened? How come that Mr. Izetbegovic became the president of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: I only know what I read in the press and what I read as communication of the body in charge of the -- of counting of votes in the elections. According to that, Mr. Abdic received the biggest number of votes, but I really don't know what happened in the SDA among the leaders of the SDA who decided that it would be Izetbegovic who would become the most prominent figure.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As the director of the mine, did you report to the government of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: No. Not to the government. I didn't report to the government. However, we had to intervene very often when we couldn't pay salaries, when there were strikes in the mine in 1991. So we had to intervene with a prime minister. I believe his name was Pero Pehlivan. I had contacts with him on two or three occasions. And I was also received by Mr. Cengic. I was in the delegation of the Ljubija Trade Union. We appealled to his authority and asked him to have a word with the bank of Zenica and asked them to pay for the iron ore that was delivered to Zenica. All the transactions went through that bank. Mr. Hrle was also present at that meeting. He was the president of the trade union of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On page 19, line 16, there is a name Pero. And I believe that you said Pehlivan.

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Correct. Pehlivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In 1991 and in 1992, did you notice -- did you observe that there was a migration of the population, and where were people headed for?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: At the beginning of 1991, this did not occur, and I couldn't see it or feel it. Bearing in mind my role and my position, I did not really pay too much attention to any such events. However, in late 1991, I did see that the families of my friends started leaving. Those were mostly women and children and elderly people. I'm going to give you an example hoping that my friend, whom I'm going to mention, will not hold it against me. Emir Kulenovic was my good friend. We visited each other. And he was the one who sent his family away sometime in late 1991 or early 1992. Eso Tadic left the area in May. He left Prijedor in May, although until then, we were inseparable. He never came to goodbye. I never understood why all this was going on, although I could feel the tensions and I believed that the tensions were the cause of their departure. I also thought at the time that maybe they knew more than I knew. Mr. Emir Kulenovic left Prijedor and Banja Luka with the Borac football. This is a Banja Luka-based football team. They were playing in the finals in Bari in Italy. He never gave the reason for leaving Banja Luka. I can't give you any more information on that because I was not the one who had that many friends, nor was I in the position to observe things at a larger extent. But I know of an incident that took place in a bus headed for Banja Luka. I believe that the police had to intervene, that it stopped the bus and ordered some of the people on the bus who were leaving Prijedor to return to Prijedor, to go back.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This incident involving the bus, did that happen before the 30th of April or after the 30th of April, after the takeover?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't give you a precise answer. But I didn't mention the fact that my best man, Mirko Drljaca sent his children to Belgrade at the same time. So this was not only the case of Muslims leaving, but also some Serb families, and I suppose there were also Croat families who did the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In 1991 and 1992, did you notice the arrival of refugees from Croatia?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I apologise. This has reminded me of the year 1995. But after the things that happened to Zec family in Zagreb, Serbian families started returning to Prijedor from Croatia, and they didn't bring any of their property, anything, with them. And they remained in Prijedor after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us, now that you have mentioned Zec family, what happened to them? Where is that family from?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: I believe that Zec family is from the vicinity of Prijedor. I believe that the name of the village is Dragotinja or something like that. I don't know the details. I only know what I read in the papers. And I read again two or three years ago the statement of their grown-up children who had survived. And the story was that uniformed people came, took them out of the house. And after that, they never saw their father again. I know that the family was rather well off. They were actually rich. They were a rich, Serb family residing in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the perpetrators of the crime committed against the Zec family were later on decorated, received some medals?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you know Mr. Arsic? I'm not mentioning his ranks because -- his rank because the rank changed.

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I knew him. He was, I believe, in 1990 and 1991 the commander of the garrison of the Yugoslav People's Army in Prijedor. I believe that in late 1991, he was Lieutenant-Colonel, but I'm not sure. And if you will allow me, having said that, I knew him. I had opportunity to attend meetings organised by him in my capacity as a businessman. I believe that he is a native of Serbia. He was from Serbia. He was exceptionally -- I would like to use a word "arrogant," but that is not what would describe him. He was domineering. When he issued orders, he did it in a very domineering tone. At the time that I met him, he was still not in the military. And that is probably -- I believe that the military education turned him into the man that he was. He did not put up with any discussions. He just issued orders, and he expected people to obey his orders and to deliver.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When we're talking about him, we also mentioned the sentence which he used to explain to other nonmilitary how things would develop from then on.

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: The sentence was things that he said they would be. That's why I said previously that he didn't put up with discussions. I mean, yes, the discussion was okay, but eventually, he had the last call, and things would be what he decided them to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you describe the process of the distribution of positions in Prijedor Municipality after the multiparty elections in 1990? At what level was that established, at what level was that implemented? Do you know who participated in the discussions on the distribution of positions?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: The SDS, the SDA, and the HDZ won the elections. I believe that the communists also had a small number of seats in the assembly. In conversations with my colleagues, I learned about the issues that you are asking me about. The assembly was convened, and after that, the executive branch of the government had to be established; that is, the Executive Board of the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor. There were secretariats which did the work in the municipality, and the parties proposed their candidates for certain positions. The discussions lasted for a long time. And I know from conversations that Srdjo Srdic participated on part of the SDS in these discussions, that there was also Dr. Milan Kovacevic, and I believe Simo Miskovic, who was the president of the SDS at the time. Whether there were any other people representing the SDS, I don't know. Again, from conversations, I know that Dr. Mujadzic participated on behalf of the SDA, and that -- and I don't know who represented the HDZ in those discussions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Would it be a convenient time, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Indeed, it would. The trial stays adjourned until 10 minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. The Defence may proceed with the most concrete and most relevant questions immediately, please. Continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, first of all, we have the obligation to tell you the numbers of the coming witnesses for this week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's number 079, 066, 070, and 006.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for this information. Taking this into account, as mentioned before, we discussed it briefly during the break, if you can concentrate on the relevant questions, relevant for this case, not relevant for the situation in former Yugoslavia. But I think you understand what I want to say by this because of the witness. So please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Marjanovic, you were appointed the CEO of the mine on the 1st of February, 1991, as you've told us. Were there attempts to remove you in 1992 after the 30th of April?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were attempts on the part of some leaders of the SDS. I was not the only target of that. There were a number of company directors who were targeted at the time. Later on, two or three company directors were removed by these people. I remained in my position as the director of the mine, and I don't have any explanation for that. The director of Energopetrol was removed. His name was Radomir Bursac. The director of the post was removed. His name was Marko Pavic. I know about the two of them. If there were any other changes, any other removals from positions, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At that time, was Mr. Sidjak appointed to any of the leading positions?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: I know Mr. Sidjak. He was a member of the SDS, and he was appointed later on in a later stage as the director of Energopetrol. Some month or two months later, he was arrested for a fraud. They embezzled about 400.000 German marks in one way or another. So these people from the SDS, they did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: After the 30th of April, 1992, did you hear that immediately after that date, there was a murder?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: I think there was a murder in mid-May. I don't know the exact date. This was the murder of a reserve policeman in the Prijedor area at the border of Cereci and Urije, but I've forgotten the man's name.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: After this murder, did the police take their revenge against the civilian population? Did you hear anything of that sort?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: No. This didn't happen. There was an investigation. I don't know what the result of the investigation was. But at least I think so, things were done by the book. The legal procedure was followed, according to the then-valid legislation of the Municipality of Prijedor and the police rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you hear whether the police killed someone in order to retaliate, to take revenge, for this murder?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: No. I'm sure this didn't happen because since I heard about the murder of this policeman, I would have heard of other events had they occurred in Prijedor. I think there were no incidents of any sort, let alone revenge of this kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So we have started discussing the period after the 30th of April, 1992. Mr. Marjanovic, yesterday, you handed over to us some documents. They have not been translated. And therefore, I would like to ask you to read to us first the document that was read out as an announcement on Radio Prijedor after the takeover of power, and to tell us, first of all, how you came by this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Provisionally D56B.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Marjanovic, is this the document which you identified to us as a document containing the announcement read out on the 30th of April, 1992, on Radio Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is the document, and it fully corresponds to the text that was read out on Radio Prijedor. And I received this document from the journalist Rajlic who worked in the mine as a journalist and who later went to work in the Kozarski Vjesnik press centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would you please tell us when he left the mine in order to work in Kozarski Vjesnik.

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: It was probably two or three years before this.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When did you receive the document which is before you from Mr. Rajlic?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: On the same day that it was read out on Radio Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would you now be so kind as to read this document to us slowly so that all of this will be interpreted and entered into the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I just for clarification ask you when did you receive this document? You just told us it was the same day. When the same day, morning --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was on the 30th of April in the course of the day. It was around 11.00 a.m. or 12.00 noon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "To the citizens of the Municipality of Prijedor: A year and a half has already elapsed since the first multiparty elections, and the constitution of a multiparty municipal parliament or assembly and other municipal organs. And we still have a single party and single ethnic government in the municipality. "Due to the fact that the Party of Democratic Action all this time did not wish to share power, either with the winning parties or with the opposition parties, the work of the Municipal Assembly has been blocked, and the work of all other organs of government has been blocked. And because of this, the citizens and peoples of the municipality of Prijedor are living in a state of anarchy, insecurity, poverty, and great fear, and this is not all. The large companies in Prijedor are being intentionally destroyed. The work of all social institutions is being obstructed, as is the work of all public services. The sowing and reaping of crops is being hindered, as are supplies of staple foods for the citizens, while at the same time the public is being misinformed and told that negotiations are underway on sharing power. "The dozens of solutions achieved during negotiations among the three ruling parties have been obstructed by the leadership of the Party of Democratic Action whose leaders, acting through their people in the government organs and financial institutions, are looting the Municipality of Prijedor on a large scale. There have even been attempts to disassemble and take away whole factories from Prijedor and taking them off to other areas. There has been a great deal of blackmail. There have been demands for foreign currency for the Party of Democratic Action and its leaders to be paid so that they would leave individual socially-owned and privately-owned companies alone, because not even the minimum conditions for work have been provided for the companies. The citizens have been left without any means of earning their living. Workers are jobless and are not receiving their wages while old-age pensioners have lost their pensions. And the citizens have lost their savings, their health insurance, as well as legal and physical security, which has all led to the breakdown of life in general of the people in our municipality. "A great deal of tension has been caused in the past 30 days intentionally and for certain purposes, purposes pertaining to a special psychological war. And this has been caused by the organised departure of the Muslim population from Prijedor, especially women and children who have left for Croatia, Slovenia, Austria, and Germany, where they spread lies saying that they were fleeing massacres being prepared for them by the Serbian people. Dozens of buses full of young Muslim men have gone to Austrian centres for military training under the pretext of going to work abroad. This has intensified fear of the imminent war in our municipality. "The last straw was on the 29th of April, 1992 when the so-called Ministry of Defence of the Ministry of the Interior of the so-called sovereign Bosnia and Herzegovina, when a dispatch arrived with an order to the municipal secretariat for the interior and the secretariat for national defence as well as the Territorial Defence staff to the effect that in the Prijedor Municipality, they should immediately block communications, military barracks, and military facilities to mount attacks on the JNA, to take away from them weapons and technology, all of which would mean war, death, destruction, and arson in our municipality. "On several occasions, Nijaz Durakovic, the president of the socialist democratic party, has called on his members, the members of his party, to wage a war against Yugoslavia, the regular JNA, and thus, the Serbian people, which is unacceptable for all citizens of goodwill. For all these reasons, we have decided to take over power in the Municipality of Prijedor and, therefore, to take over full responsibility for the peaceful and secure life of all citizens and peoples in our municipality, the protection of their property, the establishment of the rule of law, the organising of the economy, and normal life in the town and in the villages in the area of the municipality. "We wish to tell all the citizens of the Municipality of Prijedor that in our peaceful Kozara area, we must never again experience war and slaughter, burning and destruction, charred homes, screams of terror, which is the aim of the fanatical and slavish rump leadership of Bosnia-Herzegovina. For this reason, we must remain calm, reasonable, continue living and working, and establishing normal life and work, all of which has been disrupted by the single party and single nationality authorities of the Serbian" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter correct herself, of the Party of Democratic Action.

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: "Companies must continue to operate. Communications must be passable and safe. Supplies must be normal because poverty, misery, fear, the brandishing of arms and psychological exhaustion must end. With this end in view, this government is taking over all functions and responsibility for normalising the situation and life in general on the area of our municipality. In this way, we shall make a big contribution to the solution of the crisis in Bosnia and Herzegovina and the negotiations which are underway. "Dear citizens, peaceful, safe, and protected life and property for each individual are the highest values we have been building up for 50 years in freedom. Therefore, join us and help us to defend all this and preserve it from all those who wish to push us into war, death, and desolation. For this reason, let us continue working normally in all companies, institutions, organs, public services, and all the other areas where we work and live. We must finally begin to live and work in the freedom and democracy that we have opted for in the multiparty elections. "In Prijedor, on the 30th of April, 1992, the new leadership and government of the Municipality of Prijedor."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] I would like the usher to show the witness Exhibit Number D6, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Marjanovic, have you ever seen this document before? And if you haven't, say so.

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: I have never had an opportunity of seeing this document before.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This document is an order which arrived on the 29th of April, 1992 through the communications system within the MUP, the Ministry of the Interior. Can you read this silently to yourself, and then tell us whether this might be the dispatch referred to in the announcement we have just read.

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: I have heard about this document from my conversations with my associates, and I have even heard that this document happened to fall into the hands of the leadership and the Serbian people. It is my opinion that this is the document referred to in the announcement of the 30th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Will you kindly read the date on this dispatch.

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: The MUP, the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, number 10-70, the 29th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And who signed it, please.

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: The minister of the interior, Alija Delimustafic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At that time, was Mr. Delimustafic actually the minister for the interior?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I'm sure he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As regards the announcement that you have just read out to us, did you hear from the man who gave you this document who was actually behind this announcement? I don't mean behind the dispatch.

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: It was the party, the SDS party, that was behind this announcement. And the man who gave me this, the journalist, was also a member of that party.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At that time, when the announcement was aired, do you know whether there was the Crisis Staff of the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: No. There wasn't a Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We'll go back to the Crisis Staff later. For the time being, we won't need the document, so can I please ask the usher to take them away. Mr. Marjanovic, immediately after the takeover, did representatives of the MUP come to your company? If they did, what did they tell you about your duties at work?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: In the morning, on the 30th of April, 1992, I was called, I received a call, at 5.00 in the morning, and I was told to come to the administrative building. They didn't tell me why I was supposed to go there. They just told me it was urgent. I went to the administrative building, and I found there some people in uniforms. I didn't know any of them. There were both police uniforms and military uniforms. One of the men asked me if I was the director of the mine. When I introduced myself, he informed me that the SDS had taken over Prijedor and that we should continue working as before, that all the employees should continue working. And they also asked me to be in the corridor, at the entrance, to the company building at 7.00, that is, at the time when the employees were arriving at work. To continue this line of thinking, let me tell you that all the employees came to work normally; however, two of my managers objected to the presence of the police in the corridor. We explained to them what had happened, and then they went to their respective offices. Through my secretary, I informed the production floors in Omarska, Tomasica, Ljubija, and the central workshop and all the others that we have already identified, I informed all of them that there had been a takeover by the SDS and that they should continue working normally. The majority of the employees obeyed that, observed that. The only people who didn't observe that information were the employees of maintenance and repair services. Their director was Esref Crnkic. In the previous period, his office was the place where the meetings of the Executive Board of the SDA used to take place. He was related to the president of the SDA, Mr. Mujadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On that day and on the following days, that is, before the outbreak of the conflict, did you dismiss or fire anybody from the company?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't dismiss anybody. I didn't fire anybody. In order to have an overview of the work force, I asked the directors of all the production floors and services, as well as all the secretaries, to deliver the lists of the employees of those who worked, who were on military training or who were on paid leave. We did that up to the 6th or 7th of May, and then we stopped with that practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did anybody after the 30th of April, that is, after the takeover, anybody from the new government order you to fire any of the employees? After the 30th of April, did anybody issue an order to that effect?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: No. No such order was issued. They actually asked for all the employees to remain in their jobs. It was for that reason that I asked my directors to send me the list of employees that I have just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You have also given us a group of documents which corroborate what you have just told us, the records of the employees who were present at work on any given day.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] The documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Marjanovic, we're dealing with a number of documents here. Would you kindly give us firstly the date on the top of the document and try to identify it and help us find a document that you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: The first document is DPRZ Ljubija/Prijedor. The economic unit at the clay mine of Crna Dolina, the list of employees who were supposed to work on the 4th and the 5th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a moment. Let all of us try and find the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Can the usher please put the document on the ELMO so the rest can find the same document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: This would be provisional D57B.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Marjanovic, could you please tell us what this document is all about.

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: The document is the original. Everything is original but the highlighted names of certain persons. And the person who signed this document is Ivo Komljenovic. He was the technical manager of the economic unit. He was a Croat and a neighbour of mine. In mid-1992, he went to Germany together with his family. He stayed there with his brothers and he worked there. Currently, he resides in Zagreb. This document shows the multi-ethnic composition of the work force. Also, the document shows under 5.5 which of the employees were on paid leave. There were a total of four employees on paid leave. This would be my comment of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you please give us -- put the next document on the ELMO, the next document that you are going to talk about.

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: This document arises from the joint functions of the mine. And more precisely, this is the development sector. This is the list of employees who turned up for work on the 4th of May, 1992. The development sector consists of a number of services, and these services are identified here in this document. First of all, there is the geological service on page 1; mining measurements on page 2; investment also on page 2; design on page 3; technology, I believe that it is on the same page; and finally on page 4, organisers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: On this bundle, we received together this additional fifth page.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Would the usher be so kind and turn the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And what is on the last page?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Common functions, development sector, the list of workers who failed to turn up for work on the 4th of May, 1992. Geological services, three people did not turn up for work because they were on annual leave. Mining measurements --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. Out of the three who did not come to work that day because they were on annual leave, what is the ethnic background of the person under number 1, Marko Iveljic?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Marko Iveljic is a Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What is the ethnic background of the person under number 2, Miroslava Spasovic?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Miroslava Spasovic under 2 is a Serbian lady.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And now under number 3, what is the ethnic background of Alma Muranovic?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Under number 3, Alma Muranovic is a Muslim lady.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please continue explaining page number 5 to us.

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mining measurements, one person did not come to work, Milan Dragic, who was on military training.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. Who was it who was recorded as being on military exercise or military training?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Military training was the situation that was recorded when people were mobilised.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Why did you then say that they were on military training?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: We were told by the department of defence that people were being sent for military training, and we were supposed to pay them, give them salary, which was later on reimbursed by the military, by the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now, the two people from the design department.

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mustafa Biscevic under number 1. He called in -- somebody called in and said that he was in Bjeljina and that he was asking either for a paid leave or an annual leave. Under 2, Ilijaz Drobic, he called in and asked whether he was supposed to come to work. He was told that he could take paid leave, and he subsequently called in to say that he was on his way to work, that he would come to work.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us, what is the ethnic background of these two men?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: They are both Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you please continue.

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Technology, four men. Simo Karan, military training of the Territorial Defence. Zeljko Mlinar, military drill of the Territorial Defence. Dragomir Vrucinic, military drill of the Yugoslav People's Army. And handwritten addition, Drago Anic, military drill of the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Kindly read again the names of these people again and tell us their ethnic background.

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Under 1, Simo Karan is a Serb. Under 2, Zeljko Mlinar is a Croat. Under 3, Dragomir Vrucinic is a Serb. As for Drago Anic, I'm not sure whether he is a Serb or a Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Before we mark this document provisionally, we can see that -- and no doubt, the first four pages seem to be one document. The fifth page doesn't show on the top of the page the number "5." Could you please tell us, was this one document, or was the fifth page added to the previous document?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] If I may assist --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please let --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you please take the document in your hands and look at it.

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: This document is an original, and it arrived at my desk in this form. I don't know what the director of the development sector added to this document subsequently, why did he not put the page number on the page containing the list of workers who failed to show up for work. But I believe, and it is my testimony, that the last page of this document is an integral part of the original document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So the entire document containing five pages would be provisionally marked D58B. And that we do not have to return to this document, may I just ask, on the fifth page, one can read "Milan Dragic." I know there are a number of persons with the second or the final name Dragic. Do you know by chance a Milovan Dragic? Is it one and the same person or a relative, sibling, to Milan Dragic? Page 5, Rudarsko Mjerenje.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know Milovan Dragic, but this is not that same person. This person here is a driver in this particular service in the mining measurements and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Do you know whether or not this Milan Dragic is a relative to Milovan Dragic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for this clarification. Please proceed. If it's -- maybe it's appropriate to have the break now. The trial stays adjourned until 1.30. --- Luncheon recess taken at 11.59 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. Please, Mr. Lukic, proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would the usher be so kind and place another document on the ELMO so we know which one Mr. Marjanovic is talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Is it correct, there's one document, one page only?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Because one can see that there had been a document attached to this previously.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That was a copy, so we stapled everything together, and probably one is taken off. So Your Honours can look at the original which is in front of Mr. Marjanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We come back to this later when we discuss the admission into evidence. This would be marked provisionally D59B. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you once again, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Marjanovic, would you please explain what this is about, this document.

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: This document was drawn up on the 4th of May, 1992, by the head of the mining sector, Mr. Ibrahim Pahunovic, a graduate engineer, and the sector is the mining sector. It's a list of employees in the sector and the status on the 30th of April and the 4th of May, 1992. Under number 1 is Ibrahim Paunovic who worked and continued to work until the 4th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. When you say worked until the 4th of May, 1992, does this mean that his employment was terminated on that date, or that he worked on both days, the 30th of April and the 4th of May?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Here it says clearly under number 1, Ibrahim Paunovic, and this is the report for the 30th of April, 1992, and it says here that he worked, that he was present at work on that date. And then in the next column, it says work on the 4th of May, 1992. Under number 2, Djuric, Ljubomir, Ljubomir Djuric, it says military exercise on the 30th. And then he returned and worked until the 4th of May. Zora Bilbija was on annual leave, and her annual leave continued. Muhamed Mujagic worked and will continue to work. Tinka Knezevic was present at work and will continue to be so. Under number 6, Esad Pasagic on paid leave, and he reported from his paid leave. Semsa Novakovic under number 7 was present at work, and then the next column says annual leave. Mirzeta Halilovic was present on the 30th, and then in the next column it says annual leave. Gordana Manojlovic was on paid leave, and she reported from her paid leave. Cedna Puric was on paid leave, and she reported. She called in. And then in the note, it says: "The following are on paid leave: 1, Esad Pasagic, Gordana Manojlovic, and Cedna Puric." And then it was signed for the mining sector by Ibrahim Paunovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I apologise, but we shall have to go through this again so that you can tell us the ethnic affiliation of all these persons, the first group of ten employees, then the next group of three, and also the ethnicity of the person who signed this document.

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Under number 1, Ibrahim Paunovic is a Muslim. Number 2, Ljubomir Djuric, a Serb. Number 3, Zora Bilbija, I'm not sure whether she is a Serb or a Croat. Muhamed Mujagic under number 4 is a Muslim. Tinka Knezevic, number 5, a Serb lady. Six, Esad Pasagic, Muslim. Number 7, Semsa Novakovic, a Muslim lady. Number 8, Mirzeta Halilovic, a Muslim lady. Number 9, Gordana Manojlovic, a Serb. Number 10, Cedna Puric, a Serb. In the note, numbers 1, 2, and 3, they are all in the above table, but I can repeat. Esad Pasagic is a Muslim. Number 2, Gordana Manojlovic a Serb lady. And number 3, Cedna Puric, a Serb lady. And the signature for the mining sector is a Muslim, Ibrahim Paunovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we please go on to the next document. First, would you please put it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Is this document composed of two pages? Correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us whether this is a two-page document.

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's a two-page document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: This would be provisionally D60B.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Marjanovic, is this a work plan as to who was supposed to be at work over the next few days?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: This was a report drawn up in the development sector on the 23rd of April, 1992. And it's a list of employees who are to be at work from the 27th of April to the 1st of May, 1992. So that this is actually a plan for the work force for this period in the development sector, geology.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, but in order to avoid going back again, but as soon as you read out a name, could you please tell us the ethnicity if you know.

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Geology, number 1, Zvonko Leskur, a Croat. Number 2, Ljubinko Protic, a Serb. Number 3, Ruzica Mrdja, a Serb lady. Dubravko Besic, number 4, a Muslim. Geographical land surveying, Sveto Kovacevic a Serb. Design, Number 6, again, it's clearly visible. Andjelko Lovric, a Croat. Investment construction, Dusan Milosevic, a Serb. And number 8, Mirjana Pijak, I'm not sure what her ethnicity is. Technology: Number 9, Idriz Crnic, a Muslim. Number 10, Marko Begic, a Croat. Number 11, Jozefina Bujic, a Croatian lady. Organisers: 12, Tode Jakouljevic, a Serb. 13, Bahra Kadic, a Muslim lady. 14, Zineta Sahuric, a Muslim lady. 15, Tonka Asdukovic, a Croat lady. Page 2 is a report of the development sector drawn up on the 30th of April, 1992. And it's a list of employees who were present at work on the 30th of April, 1992. Geology --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think we need not go through this entire document because the names primarily are repeated. We have just additional names, and it would call for an explanation why on this 30th of April, there were more people at work than planned. If you could, when comparing both documents, give us the explanation of -- this explanation and the additional names. So, for example, under geology, you will find number 5 and 6 in addition. Number 8 -- number 7 in addition.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Marjanovic, would you please take the document so that you can compare both pages, the previous page containing the plan, and the page we are looking at now, so that you can see which names are the same on both lists. Geology, numbers 5 and 6 have been added.

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: It says Zeljko Ljustina, a Croat. And 6, Petar Balaban, a Serb. I assume that they reported to work on that day in spite of the plan. Zeljko Ljustina is a geologist, and Petar Balaban is a driver. I assume that they went to look at the field, the well. Mustafa, a Muslim, Mustafa Dzafic, a Muslim, geodetics, he reported for work I assume because he was to survey the existing excavation sites, and he was a land surveyor. This is done every month.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would you now please take the next document. How many pages does the document on the ELMO have?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. This is a three-page document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Provisionally marked D61B.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would you please explain what this document is about.

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: This document was drawn up in the development sector, and it's a list of employees who will not be working in May.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We'll go through it again in the same way. So will you please read the name and tell us the ethnicity and then the reason.

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Geological service: Marko Iveljic, from the 5th of May to the 30th of May -- Marko Iveljic who is a Croat, from the 5th of May to the 30th of May, annual leave and paid leave for part of the time. Number 2, Branko Glusac, a Serb. From the 5th of May to the 30th of May, paid leave. Miroslava Spasovic, from the 5th of May to the 30th of May -- I apologise. Miroslava Spasovic, a Serb lady, from the 5th of May to the 30th of May on annual leave and part of the time on paid leave. Miroslava Batoz, a Serb lady, from the 5th of May to the 30th of May, paid leave. Ranko Cvijic, a Serb, from the 5th of May to the 30th of May, military exercise. Milena Tanasic, a Serb lady, and now, the dates are all repeated from the 5th of May to the 30th of May, paid leave. Jasna Gligic, a Croatian lady, from the 5th of May to the 30th of May, paid leave. Pero Balaban, a Serb, from the 5th of May to the 30th of May on paid leave. Branislav Blazic, a Serb, from the 5th of May to the 30th of May on paid leave. Vladimir Razbusek, a Croat, from the 5th of May to the 30th of May on paid leave. Mersija Besirovic a Muslim lady, from the 5th of May to the 30th of May, paid leave. Number 12 Mladena Kesic, from the 5th of May to the 30th of May, paid leave. Svjetlana Sinanovic, a Serb lady, from the 5th of May to the 30th of May, paid leave. 14, Stepica Iveljic, a Croat lady, from the 5th of May to the 30th of May, paid leave. 15, Alma Muranovic, a Muslim lady, on sick leave. 16, Ante Zunic, a Croat, from the 5th of May until the 30th of May on paid leave. 17, Muhamed Hadzic, a Muslim, from the 5th of May to the 30th May, paid leave. 18, Ljilja Dobras, a Serb lady, from the 5th of May to the 30th of May, paid leave. 19, Ahmed Mujagic, a Muslim, from the 5th of May to the 30th of May, paid leave. Number 20, Mugdim Islamovic, a Muslim, from the 5th of May to the 30th of May, paid leave. 21, Bojan Ecim, a Serb, from the 5th of May to the 30th of May, paid leave. 22, Zeljko Ljustina, a Croat, on completion of his task to demolish the bunker, paid leave. I have to clarify this. I mean, the demolition of the bunker. The old Ljubija plant had a bunker for loading ore. And this was made of wood, which was in use until the 1960s. For lack of maintenance, it was in danger of collapsing and falling across the railway tracks of the railway station in Ljubija. That's why it says "on completion of this task." The investment construction service, 1 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I just interrupt, if the parties agree, we can, I believe, omit to read out the following names. I think we all can agree that we find a list of names composed of all different ethnicities we can find in the third column the dates, the fourth column the reasons why they are not present. It can also be agreed, so it need not be read out save the last three lines on page 3. Prosecution, any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. If you would be so kind and read out on page 3 the last three lines.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Due to the lack of the blueprint Blank pages inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Pages 11671 to 11680. paper, especially in the mining design service, but also in other services, the majority of tasks which were started in April could not be completed. The problem persisted in May." The head of the development sector reports on the lack of - I would call it production material for their work. This is the blueprint paper on which land surveying document are printed, the mining plans and similar things. So it says here that the problem is -- predominantly can be felt in the mining design.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Marjanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Before leaving this document, may the original please be shown to the Prosecution and to the Judges. I think we can agree that we have a document before us not signed and bearing no date. Agreed?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Maybe we could ask the witness to explain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please.
