utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Perhaps I could just note, I think the transcript should reflect the original document shows what I know as White Out. Some names have been corrected with a correction fluid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think before admission into evidence, we have to go through the same procedure we did with the Prosecution document. Whenever there is a doubt, we would need either the original be presented to the Registrar or we have a colour copy from these documents. Once again the question, if you could be so kind and give an explanation why this document doesn't bear a signature and no date.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was the director of development sector until 1989. And I received this document from my colleagues, from my colleague that I worked with. This document is original, and believe me, I didn't insist on the document being signed by anybody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The question is merely based on the fact that other documents that have been read out in the past we found either in part a signature or, another document, a stamp and signature. But here, it's only for the record we can't find a stamp and we can't find a signature. It's the same as we had it in the past with other documents tendered by the Prosecution. But may the document please be handed -- given back to the registry. Thank you. So please continue with what shall be the next document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Marjanovic --

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: The next document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I apologise. Before we continue --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: This would be a three-page document and be provisionally marked D62B. This is a document of the 5th of May with the registration number 45/92. So please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The document was drawn up in the sector for market and sales on the 5th of May, 1992. Under number 45/92, this is the list of employees who were absent in the month of May of 1992. So this is the period between the 1st and the 5th of May, 1992. Organisers: Zoran Denkic [phoen] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry, can we proceed the same way that there's an agreement that we have a list of names before us, all ethnicities represented, then only one further column given the reasons for the presence or absence. Could you please briefly explain in order to avoid that we read out the entire list of names. For example, we can read Placeni Dopust. What does it mean? It would be the same as previously, that these persons were on paid leave. Correct? If you could please answer and not only nodding, because on the transcript, we can't see it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The end of April, May, and later on is the time when there is less and less work in the mine because there was no longer delivery of iron ore to Zenica. At the time, the mine had 4.600 employees. And when an employee is on paid leave, that means that the person is sent home and stays home and is paid for the time that he or she is at home.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Okay. Can we agree that it is not necessary to go through the list of all the names?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] We don't have any problems with that proposal, only maybe the rest of the reasons for the absence might be explained. And maybe it would be also interesting that there are Muslims under military service, so that's why this these documents --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Okay. When there are additional reasons, please. But then it might be helpful if you can concentrate on these persons, if you have anything additional you regard as of relevance. And no doubt, finally we need the "rekapitulacija" at the end of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you please turn to page 2, Mr. Marjanovic. The Prijedor warehouse, under 3, can you please read the name, give us the ethnic background of the person, and the reason of absence.

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Under 3, Hamdija Handzic, a Muslim, military drill, military service.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Number 11.

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: 11, Muhamed Delic, Muslim, military drill.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At the bottom of this page, we see the warehouse, the incoming goods, warehouse under 2.

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Milorad Zdjelar, a Serb, military drill.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And can you now read on page 3 the summary.

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: The total number of workers in marketing and sales, 112. Annual leave, 3. Paid leave, 24. Military drill, 14. A total number of absent employees, 41.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Has this document been signed and certified by a stamp? And is this a stamp of your company?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: This is the stamp of the socially-owned company iron ore mine, the stamp number 5 belonging to this sector, that is, to the head of the sector. And the head of the sector was Nenad Marjanovic who also signed this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And may we then have a look to the left-hand part, to the distribution. Can you tell us what we can read there and please add the name of the corresponding persons.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Sent to:" One copy to the director general, Ostoja Marjanovic. One copy to the payroll. That is the service which dealt with the payment of salaries. There were a number of employees in that service. I can't give you all of their names. One copy to the personnel. In the personnel service, I believe that the head was Munib Catic. The next addressee is director. This was the sector for common affairs. And the director of common affairs was Smail Zahirovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you please give us the ethnic background of that gentleman.

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: He was a Muslim. Smail Zahirovic was the director of that service, and he was a Muslim. One copied to all the heads of services within the marketing and sales department, there are several services. There are sales, purchase, there is a warehouse and so on and so forth. I don't know the names of the heads of these services. And finally, files.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Can we conclude D62B.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] I just have one more question to Mr. Marjanovic regarding this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you were to sign something, would the stamp be the same? Would it be the same stamp with number 5 next to your name, next to your signature?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: If I was to sign any document, the stamp would bear number 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Why would the stamp bear number 1?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: The production floors had their own stamps. Sectors had their own stamps, and each of those stamps bore a different number. In the personnel, all the heads and directors of production plants and services were assigned a stamp, and they had to sign for those stamps. According to the book of rules, it was prescribed who is allowed to sign a certain document and what stamp were they supposed to put next to their names.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Marjanovic. Does this document contain a handwritten page, or is that an entirely different document?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: This one-page document is the list of workers of the department for personnel and legal affairs who were absent on the 4th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Just for a better understanding, we have received a two-page document, one in handwriting, one in typewriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] I was confused also, Your Honour, but obviously those are two documents. But we just stapled it that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So they should be severed and treated as two --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: -- different documents okay. Then the following document would be provisionally marked D63B. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it necessary, Your Honour, that the previous document is shown to the Prosecution, the original one, and the Court?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think we shall go through all the documents later when it comes to the admission in evidence, and let's decide what we need in photocopy and colour copy. Okay, let's continue with the document D63B.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Marjanovic.

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: The list of the employees of the department for legal, personal, and general affairs who were absent from work on the 4th of May, 1992. Of the employees of the department for legal, personal, and general affairs who were supposed to come to work, only Savo Bilbija, a commuter was from Ljeskari was absent. The head of department, Munib Catic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, what is the ethnic background of Mr. Catic.

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: He is a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Has this document been signed and certified?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: It has been certified by the stamp bearing number 1, and it has been signed by Mr. Munib Catic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Maybe I have misunderstood you, just for clarification immediately, this stamp bears the number 1. Wouldn't it be for you to sign a document bearing the stamp number 1?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The department for legal, personal, and general affairs by its nature deals with all the legal affairs, and this is the same stamp because I receive legal instruction from this department, from Mr. Catic, and that is why he has the right to use this stamp bearing number 1. The stamp actually is in his custody. He is the one looking after that stamp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So it wouldn't be mandatory that when we find your signature or another person's signature, that it would be combined with stamp 1 or vice versa, when we find stamp number 1, different persons could sign with this stamp. Correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Only the legal department which was my advisor service for all the legal affairs is in charge of stamp number 1. I never signed a document without that document being first initialled by him, so it is Mr. Munib Catic who had the right to use this stamp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for this clarification. Let's move to the next document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Your Honour, I think that the witness said something what's not in the transcript. I would like to ask him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you say that the document which determines the use of stamps exists in your former company? So there is a regulation on the use of stamps.

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: In the legal affairs department, there is a document on the use of stamps by all the heads of departments and production plants. And that document also lists the stamp numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please show us the following document. And can you also explain its contents. Obviously, this is a handwritten document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: This would be provisionally, that we are not confused, D64B.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This one-page document is a report provided by two different sectors or departments. One is the finance department absent on the 4th of May, 1992. Under 1, Mirjana Jelisavac, sick.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you please give us the ethnic background of all the persons.

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mirjana Jelisavac, a Serb lady, sick. Beisa Puskar, a Muslim lady, sick. Esma Sarajlic, a Muslim lady, death in the family. Milan Bundalo, a Serb, a sick child. Signed by Mirjana Supic, a Croat lady. The department for economics and organisation. Absent on the 4th of May, 1992, Nusreta Talundzic, a Muslim lady. Signed by Mirjana Dejanovic, a Serb lady.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This document has not certified by any stamp. It has been signed, though.

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, you're right, it hasn't been certified by stamps, but it has been signed by the respective heads of the departments. And I'm sure that these are their signatures.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I believe that we have now reached the last document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I still have one in front of me, on Balaban Slobodan in handwriting. This would be the next one.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] The last one, yes. The next one and the last one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: This would be composed of one, two, three, four, five pages. Correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a five-page document. And the first page is the enclosure.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: This is a cover letter, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the addressee is Slobodan Balaban.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: This would be D65B. If we could limit ourself to the first page, agreeing that we have a mixture of all -- persons from all ethnic backgrounds, and only the additional questions or answers you need from this document should be touched upon. Can this be agreed? I can see no objection. If you could please read out page number 1, the cover page, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Socially-owned company, Ljubija/Prijedor. The department for general affairs, the head of department number 129/92. Prijedor, 4th of May, 1992. To Slobodan Balaban regarding list of employees. Here enclosed please find the list of employees who will be on paid leave in May 1992. Head of department, Professor Dusan Tubin. Signed and stamped.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Marjanovic. We have now finished with this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask, you have problems or you still feel good or do you need a break?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I could have a break, I have a problems with my eyes. I've had my glasses on for too long.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then let's have the break from now on until 10 minutes to 3.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. May I ask, everything fine with you again? No problem?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, much better. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Marjanovic, I apologise for giving you such a hard time with these documents. But you brought them along, so it's your fault actually. The multiparty assembly of the municipality of Prijedor, until when did it function?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: I think it was until around the 20th or maybe the 15th or 16th of May. I can't really be precise. I think it was held on the 16th of May, the last session, I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were you present at the session of the Prijedor Assembly Municipal Assembly on the 16th of May, and what is this date connected with?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Oh, yes, now I'm sure the session was on the 16th of May in view of the fact that this is liberation day in Prijedor, the day of the liberation of Prijedor. The session was held in the large hall of the Ljubija mine. I was not a member of the assembly, but I was with the deputies who knew me, and most of them congratulated me on being appointed director of the mine, although I had been appointed sometime before. But they hadn't had an opportunity to congratulate me before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know who was at the head of the public accountancy service in Prijedor after the takeover of power?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: I can't tell you her full name because we all referred to her as Hava. And I really don't know whether it was her first name or her last name. But she was the managing director of the public accountancy service.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: For the record, would you please repeat the lady's name and tell us her ethnic background.

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Her name was Hava, and she was a Muslim lady.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know Miro Turnusek?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He was my uncle, although he's much younger than I am. But that's what he was. And he was the director of Mira, a biscuit factory which was part of the Krus enterprise from Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And what was Mr. Turnesek's ethnic background? Was he -- did he remain in his post after the takeover of power?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: It would be hard for me to tell you what his ethnicity was. I know that he was the son of people who immigrated from Czechoslovakia. I'm almost sure of it. I wouldn't be able to tell you his ethnicity, but he worked normally like everybody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were you ever present at the handover of any weapons?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: It happened a little before these fatal events in Prijedor. It was sometime between the 15th and the 20th of May. I can't be more precise than that. I went to see the secretary for agriculture in the Prijedor Municipal Assembly, Mr. Ranko Travar. And on my way in, I met an acquaintance from Cereci, from those times, and it was a long time ago, so I can't remember his name. And he was seeking to extend the deadline for the return of weapons, and I heard them talking about this at the entrance because they hadn't managed to complete that part of the job. And after that, I didn't listen to them any more. So I wouldn't know what they said.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We are now in the period between the 30th of April and the 30th of September, 1992. Do you know what regulations applied after the takeover of power, especially legislation?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: In the period between 1975 and 1979, I was a member of the Executive Board of the assembly of the Prijedor Municipality. Although I'm an engineer, I had to be familiar, at least in part, with these regulations, this legislation, and all of the legislation was drawn up, modelled on the previous legislation with a difference. The parties in the municipality nominated the secretaries of various secretariats.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know when a state of war was declared in the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: In Republika Srpska, a state of war was declared in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you describe for us an event connected to a conversation you had with Simo Drljaca in connection with your driver.

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: When I was appointed the managing director of the mine, I changed drivers. There was a Serb who was elderly, and I suggested that Faruk -- I'll remember his last name -- be appointed in his place. His last name was Bajramovic. I apologise, I'm quite tired now, so my concentration is not as good as it was. He was a wonderful man and a great friend of mine. Almost throughout all of 1991, he performed this job. Towards the end of May, I can't tell you the exact date, when we had already started asking for passes in order to get to work, Simo Drljaca showed me a document which I did not look at in great detail. And he told me that at one of the sessions of the main board of the SDA, that Faruk had been given the task of killing me. I couldn't believe that. I went back to my office. I asked Faruk to come in, and I told him this. He said: "Boss, you don't really think I could do that." And I'm sure that he couldn't do that. But in order not to create problems for him, in case the document was true, and in order to avoid having to bear this burden myself, this knowledge, we agreed mutually that he should go to the car repair unit and do his work as a mechanic. We parted as friends. And later on, Faruk went to(redacted). Before leaving, he came to see me and say goodbye.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Shouldn't the country be redacted from the transcript?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please, so. Thank you. That's page 58, line 13.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Without repeating the name of the country to which this gentleman went, can you tell us approximately when he left?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Faruk worked in the car repair service, and in his garage, he had a mechanic workshop. And as far as I can remember, he worked until the end of 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In 1992, you were the managing director of the largest company on the territory of Prijedor Municipality. Holding the post you did, were you able to influence in any way the decisions taken by the army?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: The Ljubija mine really was the biggest company in Prijedor, with a gross income of $120 million. I performed all my tasks according to the statute of the company. And there was no way I was able to influence what the army was doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would you tell us what happened in your family on the 3rd of July, 1992.

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: I had and still have two sons. My eldest son was then 18, and he went to serve in the army at that time, which was the worst possible time for that. That was the most difficult day of my life.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: I was unable to influence. There was no possibility of exerting any influence to stop him going. Why? There was a state of chaos. The war was already raging. Trenches had been dug. The dead were already being buried. I sent my son -- rather, my son went into that chaos.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you have a conflict with your wife because of this?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, of course. Like every other mother, she said: "Well, why don't you try. Why don't you try to exert some influence to prevent this?" She didn't know that this was not possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You are still wearing your son's ID around your neck.

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: I do apologise. Fortunately, he is alive. The date is inscribed here, the date that he left.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is his name on this plate?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's an amulet. It has the date, the 3rd of July, and Dejan, his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did your other son serve in the army as well?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he did. In 1994 and 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: May we continue?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you, and if so, when did you hear that a Crisis Staff of the Prijedor Municipal Assembly had been established?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: I heard that it had been established, but I couldn't tell you the exact date because it happened in the municipality. I wasn't in contact. But I think it was after the 22nd or the 23rd of May. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were you ever present at any of the meetings of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: No. I was never present at any meeting of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were you ever present when members of the Crisis Staff were on duty? Can you describe what these stints on duty were like?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. On two or three occasions. These were nighttime stints of duty. You would have to be on duty all night. And the office was in the basement next to the centre for -- early warning information centre where there were communications. I was there when Slavko Budimir was on duty, Ranko Travar, Mr. Milomir Stakic, and Sidjak was also with us. I don't know what his first name was, but he was not a member of the Crisis Staff. The work of these people who were on duty amounted to interventions when citizens reported that there was no water, that there were problems with electricity, that there were problems to do with utilities, that roads were blocked. And then they would intervene by making a phone call to the service responsible for fixing whatever was wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you ever see Simo Drljaca on duty in this way?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: No. Well, I've mentioned the people who were there when I was there. I certainly didn't see anyone in uniform, either Simo Drljaca or a soldier or anybody like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At that time, were Crisis Staffs being set up in companies?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: I couldn't say that they were, but I can tell you that we had a team in my company guarding the technology and facilities of the mine. We didn't call it a Crisis Staff, but there was such a team consisting of 10 to 12 people who were assigned to certain areas since the facilities are scattered. And it was their duty to watch over the machines and the plants. And it was quite difficult to do that because it was risky to travel at the time. There were already barricades and so on. But that's how we tried to take care of our equipment. I don't know about other companies, but in conversation with other managing directors, colleagues of mine, I learned that they used approximately the same method.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did such bodies exist even before that, or were they introduced because of the war?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Such bodies didn't exist before, but after all of these events, because of the safety reasons, because of the protection of property, that I have already mentioned, we have acted in this particular way. And I believe that it was normal given the circumstances. Wherever and whenever there is a hardship of some sort, the law provided for the setting up of bodies called Crisis Staffs in cases of natural disasters.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What was the name of the body in your company, a working team or something like that? A task force?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: It was, in simple terms, a task force or a working team.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did your task force and people in it manage to protect your facilities from looting?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: During the first stages, that was certainly one of their tasks. Protection of these facilities is a very specific task. The Ljubija mine had a technology of washing the iron ore which comprised huge facilities for sludge sediments. And there were several millions of cubic metres of sludge in those containers. We had to organise ourselves to protect the dams. And let me just give you an example, the dam in Zune. In Ljubija, there is an early warning system in Donja Ljubija in case the dam was destroyed, a huge wave would have erased everything from the surface of the earth within 5 or 6 minutes. So the population had to be alerted to know that they had to move to the highest elevation. So that was the most difficult task. The second task by difficulty was the explosives depot. I issued an order for these explosives to be handed over to the army. There is a law that regulates that. As for the other facilities, there were people who were locals, local population, who worked on the protection of the facilities in their villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: To protect the dam, did you also distribute weapons to the guards who were in charge of its protection?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. My colleague Sakib Islamovic from Donja Ljubija, a Muslim from Donja Ljubija, together with a secretary-general of the local commune in Ljubija, I know her first name. Her first name was Saha. So together with her, they agreed that some of the weapons that we had would be given to the local commune who would assign people to replace our own guards at the dam in Zune. We managed to preserve all the dams.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That dam in Ljubija would have destroyed Donja Ljubija if it had been destroyed and if it had burst. Can you tell us, what was the population of Donja Ljubija? What was its ethnic composition?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Donja Ljubija would have received the initial impact, and Donja Ljubija is predominantly Muslim with about 90 per cent Muslim population. But after that, the next village would be Ljeskare with mixed population, Croats and Serbs and Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Once again, can you repeat the name of the lady who was the secretary-general of the local commune and with whom you agreed the distribution of arms, and can you also tell us what was her ethnic background?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Her name was Saha, and she was a Muslim, a wonderful, wonderful lady.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you hear of the incident in Hambarine, and where were you at that time?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember the date of the incident in Hambarine. I believe that it was sometime between the 20th and the 23rd of May. On that day, I was in Bosanski Novi. I was on my way back home, and I heard about the conflict that had taken place. I remember the approximate date because I was supposed to go to Spain to the World Congress of Mining, and obviously I didn't go.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What did you hear about the shooting there? Who was shooting at whom, what was the demand in question? Can you explain? Can you give us some more details.

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Oh, I can just tell you what I heard from my neighbours. There was the killing of reservists at the checkpoint in Hambarine. I believe there were several wounded as well. And for a certain period of time, the dead bodies were just lying there and access was denied to them. And later on, the army took over and dealt with the whole thing in military, way so to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know who was it who asked for the perpetrators or the weapons to be handed over? What did you hear?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: I heard that it was the army who insisted on the surrender of the perpetrators. And they also said that nothing would happen. The ultimatum was rejected. I believe that at the time the commander was Zeljaja, the commander of the garrison. I believe his name was Radmilo Zeljaja.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know the name of the persons whose surrender was asked for, was demanded?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember. I can't remember. But I know he was a policeman in Ljubija. I'm tired. If I wasn't, I believe I could remember, but I don't want to waste any of your time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You're right. Let's move on. The next incident was in Kozarac on the other side of Prijedor. Did any of the mine equipment went missing or was it used at the checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: I'll try and explain what I saw and then what I subsequently heard. On the Prijedor/Banja Luka Road in the area of Kozarusa, a trailer was set on the road to block the traffic. Behind the petrol station at the crossroads to Kozarac, there was a container which was taken from the central workshop of the Ljubija mine without the approval of relevant services there. And further on towards the east, towards Banja Luka, I don't know whether there were any other obstacles. But I heard that a military convoy was headed from Banja Luka to Prijedor, and they asked for the obstacles to be removed. And I also heard that a soldier had been killed, and then all hell broke loose.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who from the Territorial Defence of Kozarac asked for the obstacles to be removed?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Not only in the area of Kozarac, but there are also barricades in other areas or villages, so to say. People organised themselves. They put up defence and inventions and suggestions came from the Crisis Staff for the obstacles could be removed so that the traffic could start moving freely. And in most cases, it bore fruit. But in this case, it was fruitless. These attempts were fruitless.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Before the arrival of this military convoy, did the army also issue an ultimatum for barricades to be removed from that Banja Luka/Prijedor Road?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: After the conflict in Kozarac, the facilities in Omarska -- your facilities in Omarska were taken and occupied. What can you tell us about the way this happened?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: The director of Omarska was Dusko Vlacina. He was director of the production plant there. And the organisation of watching the facilities in Omarska was under his authority. I learned a few days after the incident in Kozarac that the army and the police had forcibly entered the facilities in Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who was it who informed you about the forcible entry into these facilities?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: There were already stories in town. I didn't believe those stories. But people who were in charge of providing security in Omarska informed me. I can't remember their names. Those are security guards. It wasn't Mr. Vlacina who informed me about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you ever see a piece of paper, a document, that would justify the takeover of facilities in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: At that time, I did not see any piece of document that would came to me. Any such piece of paper would have been filed and recorded. The first time I saw such a piece of paper was yesterday evening. You showed it to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Before this incident, when was it the last time you visited the facilities in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: In my capacity as a director, I didn't need to make rounds of the facilities. From time to time, I would go to familiarise myself with them. I believe it was in 1991 when I went to the local commune of Omarska. There was something with the water supply there that I needed to inspect. And that's when I also made rounds of the mine facilities. And after the -- all the misfortunate events, I was again in the Omarska plant at the beginning of 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: From the moment when the facilities were taken over, could you in any way influence the developments at that site?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Firstly, let me tell you that there was no way for me to do anything, to prevent these things. I'm afraid that at that -- that if I had received a document at that time, I would have made an attempt to prevent these things from happening. And I frankly don't know what would have happened to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you go to Simo Drljaca about this, about a friend of yours?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: I had to go to the public security centre to be issued passes for the free movement of my employees. My friend, the -- my --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you explain the word.

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: So this gentleman was my brother-in-law's brother. The two of us married two sisters. So I tried to intervene with Simo Drljaca. I asked him to release one gentleman who was very popular in Prijedor, who was a private entrepreneur. The answer was yes, he could be released, but only if I accepted to take his place.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What is the name of the gentleman?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Nikola Matanovic, a Croat. When I received this answer from Simo Drljaca, obviously I didn't know what to do. I don't know what to say to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But is Mr. Matanovic still alive today?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he survived Omarska. I believe that later on, he went abroad, and he returned. And I think that he currently resides either in Vojnic or in Glina.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did Simo Drljaca also threaten to hang you?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I'll try to give you the reasons why this happened. A young man from the reserve police force was wounded in the spine, and he couldn't walk. And Simo asked the mine to provide this young man with a big house. I refused to do that because there were a number of such cases, and the house in question was unsuitable for somebody who was in a wheelchair. My idea was to give him a three-room flat in Pecani which would be adapted to suit the needs of that young man whose name was Dejan. And then Simo told me he would have me hanged, and he immediately sent the police who seized my Mercedes, the Mercedes car that I used for official purposes. Obviously he didn't have me hanged because I'm still here. So he didn't do what he threatened he would.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: After all this, what was your personal relationship with Simo Drljaca?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't know Simo Drljaca before these events, before the 30th of April. And since I was duty bound to go and fetch these passes, I got to meet him. At first, he looked absolutely normal to me. As the events developed, he proved to be absolutely unsuitable for any sort of communication. He was arrogant in his dealings with everybody. And we never struck even an ounce of friendship after these events on the 20th or the 25th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At that time, between the end of May and the end of August, what did you know about the events which were taking place within your compound in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: This was called investigation centre. There were all sorts of stories about this place. I believe that some of these stories were correct; some of them were false. There were some false statements and some truthful statements. But I am sure - I was then and I am now - that nothing good was happening up there. I received information that up there, there were some of my colleagues who had previously worked with me in the mine who had been my associates, for example, Sakib Islamovic was released after somebody from Belgrade put up a good word for him. He now works in Zenica and lives in Prijedor. There were others from the mine. What was really going on there, I didn't know then. I don't know now. I've never had any details on what was going on there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At that time, was the so-called work obligation introduced, and if it was, do you know when?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: The work obligation was introduced -- I don't know exactly when, but it was at the very beginning of June. I believe that it coincided with the introduction of a curfew in Prijedor. After that, for a long period of time, people were asked to subscribe to this work obligation. The procedure in the mine was as follows: The heads of various sectors would put up -- would draw up lists of people that they needed for providing security facilities and equipment. I would receive those lists, and I would send them to the secretariat for national defence. And it was the secretariat who approved those lists, who approved the work obligation for the people on those lists.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were there a number of people absent from the company because they were mobilised there? They were members of the army?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: According to my estimate, given the fact that the JNA also recruited people from Prijedor and those people were also sent to Slavonia, in the first part of June, over 30 per cent of the work force of the mine were militarily engaged. A vast majority were at home on standby. During the month of June, I asked people to call in so that we could compile their lists. In later stages, over 90 per cent of the total work force of the mine were militarily engaged. The only persons remained working were women and myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You said that after the takeover, people mostly remained working in the company. When I said "working," some of them were on annual leave, some were on sick leave, some reported for work. When was it that people stopped coming to work on a large scale?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: After the events which took place in Kozarac, it became impossible to have a good enough insight into the status of the work force. The mine stopped delivering the ore to Zenica, so all we had to do in the mine was maintaining the surface excavation site and pumping water to prevent flooding. That was all we had to do. So the work load was significantly reduced.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The work load was obviously reduced due to the previous events that had taken place. But did Muslims and Croats stop turning up for work after the attack on Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: After the attack on Prijedor on the 30th of May, 1992, not only did they fail to turn up for work, nobody came to work except for the team that I had set up. At that time, for my own personal security reasons, I also carried a pistol, and I had a security guard escorting me at all times. Later on, during the month of June, a lot of people moved from Prijedor. They were mostly Muslims and Croats. Therefore, obviously, they couldn't come to work. And I have to mention another thing before I forget. There was no way for me to establish the real status of the work force. I believe that this happened sometime in July, but I can't be sure. I drew up a document firing all those who had failed to turn up for work, not only Croats and Muslims but everybody. And this document also provided for the possibility for them to appeal. A number of workers of heard that, and then we were able to establish the approximate status of the work force which enabled us to continue paying salaries, to continue paying contributions into various funds, to contribute putting shifts together and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember if there was a curfew introduced in Prijedor Municipality?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was introduced. If my memory serves me well, this happened in late May and the curfew was in place until the end of June. And again, if my memory serves me well, the curfew was between 2200 hours and 6.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your building is across the road from the MUP building in Prijedor. Correct?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The headquarters of the Ljubija mine is in Mosa Pijade Street Number 1. And the MUP building is across the street, almost at right angles. From my office, one could see the entrance into the MUP building and the front facade of that building. At that time, during the month of June, I noticed and I saw a number of people, mostly women, standing in front of the MUP building. Later on, I found out that they had applied for departure documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: From your window, did you ever see people in that line being ill treated by anybody?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't see that. I think that this would have been impossible. Those were predominantly women in the line. There were a few men as well, but predominantly women who were standing in that long line waiting to enter the MUP building and to obtain the documents of some sort. I don't know what documents they were applying for. But in any case, those were the documents enabling them to leave Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I have to ask you, although one may draw a conclusion from your previous answer, did you ever see anybody in that line of people being killed by somebody?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: No, not at all. Even if I had not been looking, I would have heard because it is very close to my building, some 30 metres away from my building. So I would have heard some sort of a sound, and I'm sure that I never heard anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you see anybody having been taken away by the police from that line? Or did you ever hear of anybody from that line being taken away by the police or arrested?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: No. Never. I didn't hear of anybody from that line having been arrested. I didn't hear that; I didn't see it either.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think that the technical booth has ready one video. It wouldn't last long, but we would like to show the witness that clip.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: That should be no problem. If we can get the green light from the video booth. Yes, I can see it's confirmed. So please --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's Exhibit Number S7.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: S7. So it may be started.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Marjanovic, do you recognise -- not me, but somebody else on this picture on this frame of the video from the meeting?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. In the central part, I recognise Dr. Milomir Stakic., Slavko Budimir. To the left, I think it's Kovacevic, Milan Kovacevic. Then on the right-hand side, you can see part of someone's head. I think that's Simo Drljaca. On the opposite side, Mandic, I think his first name was Bosko. Those are the people I recognise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: For the transcript, we are now with 11:36:30:05.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Marjanovic, when the video starts again, would you tell us when to stop, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] I would ask the booth to rewind the tape so we can start a few seconds before.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now. Now can we stop now. Now it's clearer, the picture is clearer. Let me repeat. In the central part is Mr. Milomir Stakic. Next to him on his left-hand side is Slavko Budimir. On his right-hand side is Simo Drljaca. The first man on the left-hand side of the picture is Milan Kovacevic. And let me repeat, opposite him is Bosko Mandic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Can we move on, play the tape, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Stop now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: For the transcript we are now at 11:36:34:08.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The first on the right-hand side of this picture is Mr. Radmilo Zeljaja. Next to Mandic, on his right-hand side, wearing a uniform, I think that's Dr. Macura. We can go on now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Stop.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: For the transcript, 11:36:40:02.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The first at the head of the table is Simo, the president of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Simo Miskovic?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Simo Miskovic. And next to him in uniform is Slobodan Kuruzovic. We can go on now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think the witness wants the video to be rewound a little bit.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Stop.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the foreground behind Kovacevic is the secretary of one of the secretariats in the municipality, and I can't recall his name at the present. But it is him. It's his face. I can't remember his name now, but I do know the man personally. We can continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Stop. On the right-hand side with a pencil in his hand is Spiro Marmat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Go on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the foreground is Savanovic, Dragan Savanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would now like to ask you whether you recognised yourself at this meeting anywhere, in any of these pictures.

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: No. I mentioned the people I recognised. I think there were one or two or three whom I don't know, but I didn't see myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: May we conclude, then, that you were not present at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: On the basis of this videoclip, no, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] We are done with the video for now, thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You said that you were a member of the Executive Board in the 1970s.

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was a member of the Executive Board for mining from 1975 until 1979.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the 1990s, and you will tell me exactly when, you were the president of the Executive Board of the Prijedor Municipal Assembly, or the vice-president.

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: I was the vice-president of the Executive Board of the Prijedor Municipal Assembly, but on a voluntary basis, from October 1993 until the 1st of August, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know to whom the Executive Board was responsible for its work?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: In its organisation and carrying out of its duties, it was the assembly that appointed the Executive Board. And they submitted their plan of work to the Municipal Assembly. It was then adopted by the Municipal Assembly, and at the end of the year, they would have to submit a report about their implementation of the plan. And they would also submit this to the assembly. The assembly had the right to request monthly reports or more frequent reports on the work of the Executive Board. So let me conclude: Under all the relevant legislation of the time following from the constitution and other legislation, the Executive Board was exclusively responsible to the Municipal Assembly. This was valid generally and it was also valid in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was the Executive Board responsible and did it submit reports to all -- did it have any other kind of obligation to the president of the Municipal Assembly?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: No. No, it didn't. Because according to the statute of the municipality, the competences were clearly defined as to how the legislation was to be implemented, how the statute was to be implemented also. So the Executive Board did not submit any reports to the president of the assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: To whom were the secretaries of the secretariats or the heads responsible, the ones who were members of the Executive Board?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: According to the then system, the heads were ex officio members of the Executive Board, and they were responsible exclusively to the Executive Board, that is, the chairperson of the Executive Board.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: In order not to be confused and to have to come back to this question, you mentioned "the then system." We are discussing now what statute? To the best of your recollection, was it the statute dating back to 1984, or was there ever a new statute adopted in 1991/1992 or later?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't be very precise. I was referring to the legislation based on the constitution of 1974 defining local self-government. Of course, at the level of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the statute could be changed by the assembly on the initiative of the Executive Board or any other political -- political subject. But we had a statute at the time, but to be quite honest, I don't know when it was adopted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Maybe we have to come back to this issue later on. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At the time that you were president of the Executive Board, at that time, was there a head of the municipality or was this post introduced later on?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I don't think the witness indicated he was president of the Executive Board.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were you the vice-president of the Executive Board?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: May I -- I was the vice-president of the Executive Board, but this was on a voluntary basis, from October 1993 until the 1st of August, 1994. So that is clear now.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Because of the legal system.

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: The institution of the mayor was introduced in Bosnia and Herzegovina two years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So when you were the vice-president of the Executive Board, the situation was the same as in 1992 when we did not have the post of mayor, but only the Municipal Assembly as the legislative branch of government, and the Executive Board as the executive branch?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The same principle applied when I was the vice-president of the Executive Board. The legislative authorities, that was the assembly, and the Executive Board, that was the executive branch. And the same principle applied in 1988 and in 1990 and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At the time when you were a member of the Executive Board, and when you were the vice-president of the Executive Board, was it possible for the Executive Board to order or ban anything in relation to the army?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA MARJANOVIC
utterances.text: No, this was not possible because the army under the law on national defence was a separate entity with its own hierarchy and chain of command. And it was quite apart from the civilian authorities, the civilian government. But not only that, the Ministry of the Interior did not come under the competence of the Executive Board of the Prijedor Municipal Assembly. According to their hierarchy, they were responsible to a higher authority in Banja Luka and the people in Banja Luka were responsible to a higher authority in Sarajevo. So there was no possibility whatsoever for someone from the executive or legislative branches of government, and I'm talking about the municipal level now, to issue orders either to the MUP or to the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] We have now to go through some documents again. And I think that the witness is pretty tired. And if you don't mind, we break today five minutes before --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We still have to discuss the admission into evidence of two separate kinds of documents. This would be D57 through D65.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D56, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: No, I want to make a clear distinction between D57 through D65 where we have a number of employees being either present or absent for the one or other reason. What is the intention? May I ask you, would you agree that the originals you presented through the Defence to the Tribunal may stay with the Registrar, with the Court, or do you want to have these originals back when leaving hopefully during this week to your hometown?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no objection to the original documents remaining with the Court because the SDS replaced me, dismissed me in 1996, and I have no use for these documents. But I hope that you will have a use for them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Do you want to have copies for your personal use, may it serve any purpose? One never knows in the future whether this may be helpful or of assistance. Would this help you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would take the copies as a keepsake. I'm sure that I will not need them any more, but they will remind me of my former colleagues and friends.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I then ask Madam Registrar to take the necessary steps to take copies of the originals. And then, may I ask the Prosecution, are there objections to admit into evidence Documents D57 through D65B always?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: There's no objection, but I would point out in fairness to the Defence, while the witness is here, that there has been no testimony regarding D61B, nor does it appear on the document what year is being referred to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, I made some notes based on the testimony of the witness based on D61B. I think this is clear. And this should be clear. And the witness even read out page 3 of this document, the last three lines. So this shouldn't be a problem. In fact, one can't read 1992, but this would be a very of evaluation of evidence. So in principle, there are no objections. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Of course, we don't have any.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then these documents are admitted into evidence under the numbers provisionally given. And please, in order to avoid additional formal translation, I would like to ask Madam Registrar to make reference to those portions on today's transcript where we can find that what has been read out by the witness to the transcript. No doubt, whenever a party or Judges later for what purpose soever need a clear and proper translation, then we would come back to this issue. Then, in addition, separate from this, we did not yet decide on D56B. This was the alleged announcement to the people of Prijedor of the 30th of April, 1992, where the witness told us this morning that he received this document the same day between 11.00 or 12.00 in the morning. May I -- may it please the Prosecution be shown the original, and then please for the Judges. May I ask why on page 2, the words or the figures "01.05.1992." Then "GOD." With a blue marker were redacted. May the witness please be shown the original and one copy. Would you please be so kind and give us an explanation why one could read the 1st of May, 1992, on this document, page 2, and this was later, blue-marked so it's not -- no longer legible.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I was giving information in Prijedor, and when I agreed to testify, I collected these documents from my archives. And I wrote this date out of carelessness. This is a recent date that I wrote on it. And when I realised what I did done, I crossed it out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: When was it crossed out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] About 15 days ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So did you provide two documents, a copy and the original? Because on the copy, one, no doubt, can read "1st of May, 1992."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I only provided the original. Only the original copy to Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] He thinks that he crossed it out, as you can see it on a copy, and then it's blanked. So maybe you can clarify that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I would appreciate if the witness could tell us. You can see on the copy that it's still legible. 1st of May, 1992. And then on the original, it's blue-marked in a way that you can't any longer read 1st of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In Prijedor, when I was preparing this document, I was careless. I thought that this was the end of the document before I discovered that there was a third page. And I thought, as I remember that it was the 1st of May, so at home, I crossed it out. The marker is the same. And when we arrived here, I did it again on the original in a blue pen. And as for this copy, I don't know how it was made.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We can explain the other part, because we copied and bought back the original to the witness so he can follow further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May -- we have to come back to this later. My proposal is to admit both the original and one copy with the additional -1 as usual. May I ask the Prosecution, the time has run out as regards the tapes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, the tape?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The videotape. So we have to conclude as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Yes. No objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No objection on our side either, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence under these -- under this number. And the copy with an additional -1. Any other issues to be discussed immediately? I only want to invite the Prosecution, please, to be prepared to discuss tomorrow in the beginning immediately the question of the videolink witnesses. This concludes today's hearing. The trial stays adjourned until tomorrow, 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
